How I Started Getting 10x Better Results From Claude Code, And How You Can Too
A few months ago, I bought Claude Code because everyone kept saying it was the best AI coding tool available.
I opened it, asked it to build an app, and honestly… I wasn’t that impressed.
The code wasn’t terrible.
It just wasn’t anywhere near what I’d expected after seeing people online saying Claude could replace entire development teams.
For a while, I thought Claude was overhyped.
It turns out I was completely wrong.
The problem wasn’t Claude.
The problem was the way I was using it.
Like most people, I was treating Claude like ChatGPT. I’d type something vague like “build me a dashboard” or “make me a SaaS landing page” and expect production-ready software.
That’s not how the best developers use it.
Once I changed my workflow, everything changed.
The websites looked better.
The code became cleaner.
Debugging became easier.
Instead of spending ages rewriting responses, I found myself accepting Claude’s first attempt far more often.
I realised the biggest upgrade wasn’t a newer model.
It was learning how to communicate with it.
The Biggest Change I Made
The single biggest mistake I was making was asking Claude to build immediately.
Now I almost always start by asking it to plan.
Before a single line of code gets written, I’ll have Claude outline the architecture, folder structure, features, reusable components and potential problems.
That one change alone probably saved me more time than anything else.
Instead of fixing mistakes halfway through a project, I avoid making them in the first place.
The Rules That Made The Biggest Difference
These are the ten Claude Code rules that completely changed how I build software.
1. Planning Before Coding
Every project starts with a technical plan.
Claude thinks better when it knows where it’s going.
2. Breaking Projects Into Features
Instead of asking for an entire application, I build one feature at a time.
The output is far more consistent.
3. Giving Full Context
The more Claude knows about your users, goals and stack, the better the result becomes.
4. Reviewing Its Own Work
I nearly always ask Claude to review its own code like a senior engineer before I move on.
It catches issues surprisingly well.
5. Designing Components First
Reusable components save hours later.
It’s much easier than rebuilding the same thing five different ways.
6. Systematic Debugging
Rather than saying “it doesn’t work”, I provide logs, expected behaviour and reproduction steps.
Claude becomes dramatically better at solving problems.
7. Refactoring Regularly
Small improvements throughout a project are much easier than huge rewrites at the end.
8. Planning Folder Structure
Good architecture makes every future feature easier to build.
Claude is excellent at this when asked.
9. Testing Before Shipping
Generating tests early has saved me countless debugging sessions.
10. Building A Prompt Library
This was probably the biggest game changer.
Instead of writing prompts from scratch every day, I reuse prompts that already work.
That means better consistency and far less wasted time.

Five Website Prompts I Still Use
If you’ve never tried structured prompts, here are five I’ve had great results with.
1. SaaS Landing Page
Prompt
Act as a senior frontend engineer. Build a premium SaaS landing page with a modern hero section, feature grid, pricing table, testimonials, FAQ and responsive navigation. Write clean, reusable, production-ready code with accessibility, performance and mobile responsiveness as top priorities.
2. Business Website
Prompt
Create a professional website for a local business. Include a homepage, services section, about page, testimonials, FAQs, contact form and strong calls to action. The design should feel modern, trustworthy and be optimised for conversions on both desktop and mobile.
3. Portfolio Website
Prompt
Build a modern developer portfolio with a clean layout, project showcase, experience timeline, skills section, contact page and dark mode. Prioritise speed, SEO, responsive design and reusable components throughout.
4. Ecommerce Homepage
Prompt
Design a premium ecommerce homepage featuring product collections, customer reviews, promotional banners, newsletter signup and clear calls to action. Focus on user experience, trust and increasing conversions while keeping the interface clean and modern.
5. Dashboard Interface
Prompt
Build a professional SaaS dashboard featuring analytics cards, charts, tables, sidebar navigation, user settings and responsive layouts. Use scalable architecture, reusable components and a polished UI that feels like a production-ready application.
The Biggest Lesson
I don’t think Claude Code suddenly became smarter.
I simply became better at using it.
That’s an important distinction.
Most people open Claude, type a single sentence and expect incredible software in return. Sometimes that works, but most of the time it doesn’t.
The developers getting the best results usually have a repeatable process. They plan before building, provide context, break projects into smaller tasks and reuse prompts that have already proven to work.
Once I started doing the same, Claude became one of the most valuable tools in my workflow.
Why I Built My Toolkit
After weeks of refining prompts, experimenting with different workflows and seeing what consistently produced the best results, I realised I was rewriting the same prompts over and over again.
So I organised them into one place.
That eventually became The Ultimate Claude Code Toolkit.
You can grab it here: alfieprints.gumroad.com/l/xydfaa
Inside you’ll find 260 prompts, workflows and systems covering website building, planning, debugging, refactoring, deployment and much more.
the takeaway from this is: The goal isn’t to replace learning.
It’s to remove weeks of trial and error so you can spend less time figuring out what to ask and more time building software that you’re proud to ship.
